This vignette covers the autocorrelation of the residuals of a plot over time, and simulation studies: simulating data from a fitted model, refitting it, and comparing the estimates with the true parameters, including the autocorrelation parameter.

## The sorghum and maize data

The data set `SorghumMaize` contains the above-ground biomass (Mg/ha) of fiber sorghum, sweet sorghum and maize at two input levels of water and nitrogen, in four blocks, sampled on 11 days of the year from sowing, day 141, to day 303 (Danalatos et al., 2009; Miguez, 2025). Each combination of crop, input level and block is a plot, sampled repeatedly over the season. The growth of a crop over a season is determinate: it stops at maturity, after which the biomass may decline as leaves are lost. The beta growth function of Yin et al. (2003), `model = "beta"`, describes this, from the start of growth $b_4$, here fixed at sowing, to the maximum $b_1$ at the end of growth $b_3$, with the time of the fastest growth $b_2$, and back towards zero after $b_3$, reaching it at $2 b_3 - b_2$ (see the vignette *Growth models and their parameters*; `model = "beta_capped"` stays at the maximum instead).

The biomass varies little between the plots while it is small, and more as it grows. A gaussian model has a constant residual variance, as large at sowing as at maturity, and data simulated from it are often negative early in the season. The lognormal family, `family = "lognormal"`, has a constant coefficient of variation instead: $\log(y)$ is normal with mean $\log f(t)$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, so that the curve $f$ is the median of the biomass, and the residuals are relative deviations from it. It needs positive responses, so the zero biomass at sowing is left out; the beta curve is zero at sowing, $b_4 = 141$, anyway. The asymptote and the time of the fastest growth depend on the crop and the input level, and each plot has a random asymptote:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)
SorghumMaize$plot <- interaction(SorghumMaize$Crop, SorghumMaize$Input, SorghumMaize$Block, drop = TRUE)
sm <- subset(SorghumMaize, Biomass > 0)
fitre <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop * Input, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = sm,
               model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal")
ggplot(SorghumMaize, aes(x = DOY, y = Biomass, group = plot, colour = Input)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Crop) +
  labs(x = "Day of the year", y = "Biomass (Mg/ha)", colour = "Input") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Autocorrelation of the residuals

A plot that is above its curve at one sampling may stay above it at the next. The `correlation` argument models this autocorrelation of the residuals within a group over time, with the same correlation structures as the package nlme (Pinheiro and Bates, 2000; Zuur et al., 2009, Chapter 6). The residuals $\varepsilon$ of a group are normal with the residual variance $\sigma^2$ and

$$\mathrm{cor}(\varepsilon_s, \varepsilon_t) = \rho^{|t - s|},$$

with $\rho$ the correlation of residuals one unit of time apart. `corAR1()` is the autoregressive process of order 1 at integer times (or at the positions of the observations, with `form = ~ 1 | group`), with $-1 < \rho < 1$; `corCAR1()` its continuous-time version, for unequally spaced times, with $0 < \rho < 1$. Residuals of different groups are independent, and the correlation is available for the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families. As the process is Markov, each residual given the previous one of its group, $dt$ earlier, is normal with mean $\rho^{dt} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{prev}}$ and variance $\sigma^2 (1 - \rho^{2 dt})$, so the likelihood is exact and its cost linear in the number of observations; with random effects, the Laplace approximation integrates them out as before.

The parameter $\rho$ is estimated on an unconstrained scale, as in nlme. For `corCAR1()`, with $0 < \rho < 1$, this is the logit link, $\log(\rho/(1 - \rho))$. For `corAR1()`, with $-1 < \rho < 1$, it is $\log((1 + \rho)/(1 - \rho))$, the logit of $(1 + \rho)/2$, which maps the interval $(-1, 1)$ to the real line (twice Fisher's $z$-transformation, $2\,\mathrm{atanh}(\rho)$). `coef()` reports the parameter on this scale, as `cor_par:CAR1` or `cor_par:AR1`, and `corpars()`, `summary()` and `confint()` report $\rho$ itself.

The plots are sampled about every 15 days, at unequal intervals, so `corCAR1(form = ~ DOY | plot)` is the structure to use, with $\rho$ the correlation per day. Its starting value is $\rho = 0.2$ by default, as in nlme, which is a correlation of $0.2^{15}$, practically zero, between consecutive samplings; there the likelihood hardly changes with $\rho$, and the optimiser stays near the starting value. A starting value close to 1, `value = 0.9`, starts from a correlation of $0.9^{15} \approx 0.2$ between samplings. For the lognormal family, the correlation is that of the residuals of $\log(y)$, the relative deviations from the curve:

```{r}
fitrec <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop * Input, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = sm,
                model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal",
                correlation = corCAR1(value = 0.9, form = ~ DOY | plot))
summary(fitrec)
corpars(fitrec)^15
anova(fitre, fitrec)
```

The estimate of $\rho$ moves far down from its starting value, to a correlation of practically zero between consecutive samplings, and the likelihood ratio test finds no autocorrelation: the relative deviations of a plot from its curve are independent over the season. The random asymptotes of the plots are not needed either, as their standard deviation is close to zero once the crops and the input levels have their own curves. With the gaussian family, both appear to be needed; this is not a feature of the plots, but of the constant residual variance, which misfits the small deviations early in the season and the large ones late. Below, simulations with a true autocorrelation show that the model finds it when it is there.

`confint()` gives the profile likelihood interval of $\rho$, or with `method = "wald"` a Wald interval computed on the logit scale and transformed back. Here it spans the whole range from 0 to 1: without autocorrelation in the data, the likelihood is flat in $\rho$, and the data say nothing about its value.

```{r}
confint(fitrec, parm = "cor_par:CAR1", method = "wald")
```

## Simulation

A simulation study has four steps: fit a model to data, simulate new data sets from the fitted model, refit the model to the simulated data, and compare the estimates with the true parameters, the estimates of the original fit.

### The true model

We fit the lognormal beta growth function to the biomass, with an asymptote and a time of the fastest growth for each crop, and a random asymptote of each plot. The start of growth is fixed at sowing, $b_4 = 141$; the beta curve has no asymmetry $b_5$.

```{r sim-fit}
fitsim <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = sm,
                model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal")
fitsim
converged(fitsim)
```

The fitted model is the true model of the simulation. Its parameters are:

```{r sim-truth}
fixef(fitsim)
VarCorr(fitsim)
sigma(fitsim)
```

Other true models can be made from it with `update()`, e.g. `update(fitsim, fixef = c("b1:(Intercept)" = 30))` for a larger asymptote of fiber sorghum, `update(fitsim, VarCorr = ...)` for another variance of the random effects, or `update(fit, rho = ...)` for another autocorrelation, as below.

### Simulating new plots

We simulate 20 new plots of each crop, each sampled every 10 days from day 150 to day 300. Each plot in `newdata` is a new curve, with its own random effect drawn from the fitted variance.

```{r sim-simulate}
simdata <- expand.grid(DOY = seq(150, 300, by = 10), plot = paste("plot", 1:60, sep = ""))
simdata$Crop <- rep(levels(SorghumMaize$Crop), each = 20)[as.integer(simdata$plot)]
simdata$Biomass <- simulate(fitsim, nsim = 1, seed = 1, newdata = simdata)[[1]]
head(simdata)
```

### Refitting the model

The same model is fitted to the simulated data.

```{r sim-refit}
simfit <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = simdata,
                model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal")
converged(simfit)
```

`converged()` checks that the log-likelihood is finite, that the optimiser reports convergence with a largest absolute gradient below $10^{-3}$, and that the Hessian is positive definite. With few groups and several correlated random effects, the likelihood is often so flat in some directions that `nlminb` reports "singular convergence" or "false convergence", or stops with a gradient slightly above $10^{-3}$, although it is at the maximum. With `control = list(restart = TRUE)`, such a fit is optimised once more from its estimates. The fit keeps the better optimum, and `fit$restart$improvement` holds the improvement of the log-likelihood. `converged()` accepts a fit that the restart improved by less than `lltol` ($10^{-6}$ by default), since its maximum is stable. In a simulation study that does not need standard errors, `sdreport = FALSE` also saves about a quarter of the time of each fit, but then the Hessian is not checked. Here, with three plots of each crop, the fit converges at once, so that the restart is not needed and `f1$restart` is `NULL`:

```{r sim-restart}
small <- subset(simdata, plot %in% paste0("plot", c(1:3, 21:23, 41:43)))
f0 <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = small,
            model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal", control = list(sdreport = FALSE))
converged(f0)
f1 <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = small,
            model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal", control = list(sdreport = FALSE, restart = TRUE))
f1$restart$improvement
converged(f1)
```

The 95% parametric bootstrap confidence intervals of the coefficients and the variance parameters are compared with the true values, the estimates of the original fit. `confint` reports the standard deviation of the random effects and the residual standard deviation on their natural scale, while `coef` has them on the log scale, so the true values and the estimates are transformed in the same way.

```{r sim-confint}
ci <- confint(simfit, method = "boot", nsim = 50, seed = 1)
natural <- function(p){
  lg <- grepl("^log_", names(p))
  p[lg] <- exp(p[lg])
  p
}
truth <- natural(coef(fitsim))
tab <- data.frame(true = truth, estimate = natural(coef(simfit)), ci,
                  covered = truth >= ci[, 1] & truth <= ci[, 2],
                  check.names = FALSE)
# the standard deviations are on their natural scale: drop "log_" from their names
rownames(tab) <- sub("^log_", "", rownames(tab))
tab
```

The simulated biomass and the estimated curves of the 60 plots:

```{r sim-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
grid <- expand.grid(DOY = seq(141, 300, length.out = 200), plot = unique(simdata$plot))
grid$Crop <- rep(levels(SorghumMaize$Crop), each = 20)[as.integer(grid$plot)]
grid$Biomass <- predict(simfit, newdata = grid)
ggplot(simdata, aes(DOY, Biomass, group = plot)) +
  geom_line(data = grid, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ Crop) +
  labs(x = "Day of the year", y = "Biomass (Mg/ha)") +
  theme_bw()
```

The simulated biomass is positive, and varies with the size of the plants, as the observed biomass does: the lognormal residual standard deviation, `r round(sigma(fitsim), 2)` on the log scale, is a coefficient of variation of about `r round(100 * sigma(fitsim))`%. A simulation study reproduces the fitted model, not the process that generated the data, so its conclusions only carry over to the real data as far as the model describes them; with the gaussian family, about a tenth of the simulated biomass values would be negative.

In a full simulation study, these steps are repeated for many simulated data sets, e.g. to estimate the coverage of the confidence intervals or to compare growth models with `criteria()`, as below for the autocorrelation.

### Recovering the autocorrelation

With a correlation structure, `simulate()` draws the residuals of each group with the autocorrelation of the fit: within a plot in `newdata`, ordered in time, each residual given the previous one, $dt$ earlier, is normal with mean $\rho^{dt}$ times the previous residual and variance $\sigma^2 (1 - \rho^{2 dt})$. `update()` is designed for simulation studies like this one: it sets some of the parameters of a fitted model to chosen values and keeps the others, without refitting, so that the result can serve as the true model of the simulation. Its arguments are `fixef` for the coefficients, `VarCorr` for the covariance matrices of the random effects, `sigma` for the residual standard deviation, and `rho` for the autocorrelation.

Here the true model is the lognormal fit `fitrec` from above, with crop and input effects, random asymptotes of the plots and continuous-time AR(1) residuals of $\log(y)$. Its autocorrelation, $\rho = `r round(corpars(fitrec), 2)`$ per day, is set to $\rho = 0.8$ with `update()`, a correlation of $0.8^{10} \approx 0.11$ between samplings 10 days apart, and all other parameters keep their estimates:

```{r sim-cartrue}
rho0 <- 0.8
fitcar <- update(fitrec, rho = rho0)
```

`update()` changes $\rho$ and nothing else, so the other parameters are those estimated together with $\rho = `r round(corpars(fitrec), 2)`$. Alternatively, a new fit with $\rho$ fixed at 0.8, `corCAR1(value = 0.8, fixed = TRUE)`, estimates the other parameters given $\rho = 0.8$. This is the way to go when the true model should fit the data as well as possible with the chosen $\rho$, and it has the higher log-likelihood; `update()` is the way to go when only $\rho$ should differ from the fitted model, e.g. to compare simulations with different autocorrelations and otherwise the same parameters.

```{r sim-carfixed}
fitfix <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop * Input, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = sm,
                model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal",
                correlation = corCAR1(value = rho0, form = ~ DOY | plot, fixed = TRUE))
pars <- function(f) c(fixef(f)[c("b1:(Intercept)", "b2:(Intercept)", "b3:(Intercept)")],
                      sigma = sigma(f), corpars(f), logLik = as.numeric(logLik(f)))
rbind(estimated = pars(fitrec), updated = pars(fitcar), refitted = pars(fitfix))
```

We simulate from the updated model: 50 data sets of 10 new plots of each combination of crop and input level, each sampled every 10 days from day 150 to day 300. We fit the model to each data set, now with $\rho$ estimated. `confint()` computes the Wald interval of $\rho$ on the logit scale and transforms it back.

```{r sim-carrun, warning = FALSE}
design <- expand.grid(DOY = seq(150, 300, by = 10), rep = 1:10, Crop = levels(SorghumMaize$Crop),
                      Input = levels(SorghumMaize$Input))
design$plot <- interaction(design$rep, design$Crop, design$Input, drop = TRUE)
sims <- simulate(fitcar, nsim = 50, seed = 1, newdata = design)
carsim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sims, function(y){
  dat <- cbind(design, Biomass = y)
  f1 <- gcTMB(Biomass ~ DOY, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Crop * Input, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = dat,
              model = "beta", start = c(b4 = 141), family = "lognormal",
              correlation = corCAR1(value = 0.9, form = ~ DOY | plot))
  ci <- confint(f1, parm = "cor_par:CAR1", method = "wald")
  data.frame(rho = corpars(f1)[["rho"]], lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
             covered = ci[1] <= rho0 & rho0 <= ci[2])
}))
```

The means of the estimates of $\rho$ and of the bounds of their 95% Wald intervals, and the coverage of the intervals, against the true value 0.8:

```{r sim-cartab}
colMeans(carsim[, c("rho", "lower", "upper", "covered")])
```

```{r sim-carplot, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(carsim, aes(x = rho)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "grey70", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rho0, colour = "red") +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Estimate of ", rho)), y = "Simulations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## References

Danalatos, N.G., Archontoulis, S.V. and Tsiboukas, K. (2009). Comparative analysis of sorghum versus corn growing under optimum and under water/nitrogen limited conditions in central Greece. In: *Proceedings of the 17th European Biomass Conference*, Hamburg, 538--544.

Miguez, F. (2025). *nlraa: Nonlinear Regression for Agricultural Applications*. R package, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=nlraa.

Pinheiro, J.C. and Bates, D.M. (2000). *Mixed-Effects Models in S and S-PLUS*. Springer, New York.

Zuur, A.F., Ieno, E.N., Walker, N.J., Saveliev, A.A. and Smith, G.M. (2009). *Mixed Effects Models and Extensions in Ecology with R*. Springer, New York.

Yin, X., Goudriaan, J., Lantinga, E.A., Vos, J. and Spiertz, H.J. (2003). A flexible sigmoid function of determinate growth. *Annals of Botany* 91, 361--371.
